<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but A more effectively exploited the central structural tension in B's proposal. A's pressure question forced B to draw a target/context line (permit human-activated interception of objects, ban autonomous hunting of people) to save systems like Aegis, and A's closing correctly identified that this line is functionally identical to the "calibrated regulation" A proposed from the opening — B never fully rebutted the charge that its own operative rule collapses the categorical/regulatory distinction it needed to defend. A also raised the proliferation-asymmetry point (China and Russia as independent leading developers, not merely downstream buyers of Western tech) and B's answer leaned on stigmatization analogies to chemical weapons and blinding lasers that don't squarely address peer-state rivals with autonomous production capacity — a gap A kept pressing through the debate. B's moral case on accountability diffusion and "error replicated at scale" was genuinely strong and under-answered by A's assertion that command responsibility "survives intact," but this alone wasn't enough to offset A's sharper, more sustained comparative pressure on verification, proliferation, and the ban/regulation collapse, which A tied together cleanly in the final speech.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's pressure question on Aegis/Patriot (turn 6) forcing B to articulate a target-and-context carve-out in B4.1, which A then used in Rebuttal 2 and Closing to argue B's "ban" had quietly become the same calibrated regulation A proposed — a move B never fully neutralized beyond asserting that functional carve-outs are consistent with what a ban is.</best_rebuttal>
